## Overview

The paper asks how fast an environment can change before a population that adapts to it
goes extinct [@Pagel2025]. Its experiments move the optimum of the fitness function by a
fixed amount every generation and record how the population responds. This vignette
looks at the ways the optimum can move, follows one population to extinction, defines
the measures the paper uses to summarise a run, and shows how the time to extinction
depends on the rate of change. The theory behind the experiment goes back to Lynch and
Lande [@LynchLande1993] and Bürger and Lynch [@BurgerLynch1995]: a population follows a
moving optimum with a lag, and the lag it can sustain is limited by its genetic variance
and by how strongly selection acts.

## Setup

```{julia}
using QTLSim
using CairoMakie, Printf, Statistics
CairoMakie.activate!(type = "png")
```

## Three ways to move the optimum

From generation `MoveFitnessSDGen` on, the optimum $\theta$ is updated at the start of
every generation, in one of three ways chosen by `MoveType`:

- `:continuous` moves it by a fixed amount, $\theta \leftarrow \theta + d$, with $d$ given
  by `MoveFitnessSD`. This is a steadily changing environment, and it is what the paper
  uses.
- `:phenotype` resets it to the current mean phenotype plus $d$ phenotypic standard
  deviations, $\theta = \bar z + d\sqrt{V_P}$.
- `:fitness` resets it to the mean plus $d$ fitness-function widths,
  $\theta = \bar z + d\omega$.

The last two keep the optimum a fixed distance ahead of the population, so the lag
$\theta - \bar z$ is set by construction and the population can never fall behind. Only
the continuous move lets the lag evolve.

```{julia}
p = Params(PopSize = 1000, Ploidy = 2, NoQTL = 100, NoGenerations = 2600,
           PhenotypeVar = 0.02, Heritability = 0.4, MutationScalar = 0.004,
           MutationRatePerGamete = 1e-4, RecombPoissonMean = 3.0, MoveFitnessSDGen = 2000)
runs = [(name, simulate(Params(p; MoveType = type, MoveFitnessSD = d); seed = 1))
        for (name, type, d) in (("continuous, d = 0.005", :continuous, 0.005),
                                ("phenotype, d = 1", :phenotype, 1.0),
                                ("fitness, d = 0.1", :fitness, 0.1))]
nothing
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-move-types
#| fig-cap: "The lag θ − z̄ between the optimum and the mean phenotype after the optimum starts moving at generation 2000. The phenotype and fitness moves hold the lag at √V_P·d and ω·d; under the continuous move the lag grows until the response to selection matches the rate of change."
fig = Figure(size = (640, 340))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel = "generation", ylabel = "lag θ − z̄", limits = ((1950, 2600), nothing))
for ((name, r), c) in zip(runs, (:crimson, :navy, :teal))
    lines!(ax, r.gen, r.theta .- r.pheno_mean, color = c, label = name)
end
axislegend(ax, position = :rb)
fig
```

## Anatomy of an extinction

The paper's populations first spend 10,000 generations under stabilising selection and
then face a continuously moving optimum. Here is one such population, with parameters
near the middle of the paper's ranges, followed until it dies out (compare the paper's
Supplementary Figure S3).

```{julia}
paperlike = Params(PopSize = 1000, Ploidy = 2, NoQTL = 100, NoGenerations = 12_000,
                   PhenotypeVar = 0.022, Heritability = 0.32, MutationScalar = 0.004,
                   MutationRatePerGamete = 1e-4, RecombPoissonMean = 3.0, InitFitnessSD = 5.0,
                   MoveFitnessSDGen = 10_000, MoveType = :continuous)
ex = simulate(Params(paperlike; MoveFitnessSD = 0.05); seed = 3)
(extinct = ex.extinct, extinct_generation = ex.extinct_gen)
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-extinction
#| fig-cap: "One population after the optimum starts moving at generation 10,000 (dashed line). (a) The mean phenotype falls ever further behind the optimum. (b) Genetic variance is eroded as survival collapses. (c) The number of individuals surviving selection each generation; the population is refilled to 1000 by the survivors' offspring until fewer than two survive."
window = (9_900, ex.extinct ? ex.extinct_gen + 10 : 12_000)
fig = Figure(size = (960, 300))
ax1 = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel = "generation", ylabel = "phenotype / optimum", title = "(a)",
           limits = (window, nothing))
lines!(ax1, ex.gen, ex.theta, color = :gray, label = "optimum")
lines!(ax1, ex.gen, ex.pheno_mean, color = :navy, label = "mean phenotype")
axislegend(ax1, position = :lt)
ax2 = Axis(fig[1, 2], xlabel = "generation", ylabel = "genetic variance", title = "(b)",
           limits = (window, nothing))
lines!(ax2, ex.gen, ex.geno_var, color = :teal)
ax3 = Axis(fig[1, 3], xlabel = "generation", ylabel = "survivors", title = "(c)",
           limits = (window, (0, 1050)))
lines!(ax3, ex.gen, ex.nsurv, color = :crimson)
for ax in (ax1, ax2, ax3); vlines!(ax, [10_000], color = :black, linestyle = :dash); end
fig
```

## The paper's measures

The paper summarises each run by a handful of numbers, all measured in units of the
phenotypic standard deviation so that populations with different variances can be
compared. With the move starting at generation $g_0$:

- **Generations to extinction** $T$: the number of generations of directional selection
  until the population dies, counting the generation in which it dies.
- **50% mortality**: the first generation after the move at which the number of
  survivors is closest to $N/2$; $T_{50}$ counts generations to it in the same way as
  $T$. The phenotypic standard deviation $s_{50}$ at that generation is the unit for
  everything else.
- **Standardised environmental change** $x = d / s_{50}$.
- **Standardised rate of phenotypic change**: how far the mean phenotype moved, per
  generation, in units of $s_{50}$, either until extinction or until 50% mortality.
- **Standardised lag**: $x$ minus the rate of phenotypic change to extinction, the
  amount per generation by which the population falls further behind.

The function below computes them from a run, following the conventions of the paper's
results table, which counts generations from one (so its "generation 10,000" is the last
generation before the move). The
[replication vignette](../09_replicating_pagel_2025/09_replicating_pagel_2025.qmd) checks
it against the table itself.

```{julia}
function paper_measures(o, p::Params)
    g0, N, d = p.MoveFitnessSDGen, p.PopSize, p.MoveFitnessSD
    sd = sqrt.(o.pheno_var)
    i0 = findfirst(==(g0 - 1), o.gen)                         # last generation before the move
    post = findall(>=(g0), o.gen)
    k = isempty(post) ? lastindex(o.gen) : post[argmin(abs.(o.nsurv[post] .- N ÷ 2))]
    T = o.extinct ? o.gen[end] + 2 - g0 : length(post)        # the last record precedes the dying generation
    T50 = o.gen[k] + 2 - g0
    x = d / sd[k]
    rate = (o.pheno_mean[end] - o.pheno_mean[i0]) / T / sd[k]
    rate50 = (o.pheno_mean[k] - o.pheno_mean[i0]) / T50 / sd[k]
    (; T, survived = !o.extinct, T50, sd50 = sd[k], x, rate, rate50, lag = x - rate)
end

paper_measures(ex, Params(paperlike; MoveFitnessSD = 0.05))
```

## How long populations last

Now the same population faces a range of rates, four replicates each, each run allowed
up to 2000 generations of directional selection. Runs are independent, so they are
spread over threads.

```{julia}
rates = [0.002, 0.005, 0.01, 0.015, 0.02, 0.03, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2]
jobs = [(d, rep) for d in rates for rep in 1:4]
res = Vector{Any}(undef, length(jobs))
Threads.@threads for k in eachindex(jobs)
    d, rep = jobs[k]
    q = Params(paperlike; MoveFitnessSD = d)
    res[k] = (; d, paper_measures(simulate(q; seed = 100k + rep), q)...)
end
for d in rates
    rs = filter(r -> r.d == d, res)
    @printf("d = %.3f   x ≈ %.3f   survived %d of 4   median T = %s\n", d,
            median(r.x for r in rs), count(r -> r.survived, rs),
            all(r -> r.survived, rs) ? "> 2000" : string(round(Int, median(r.T for r in rs))))
end
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-rate-sweep
#| fig-cap: "Generations to extinction (left) and standardised lag (right) against the standardised rate of environmental change x for one parameter set. Open circles (left) and teal points (right) are populations still alive after 2000 generations of directional selection; the others died."
fig = Figure(size = (900, 360))
ax1 = Axis(fig[1, 1], xscale = log10, yscale = log10, xlabel = "standardised rate x = d / s₅₀",
           ylabel = "generations to extinction")
ax2 = Axis(fig[1, 2], xscale = log10, xlabel = "standardised rate x = d / s₅₀",
           ylabel = "standardised lag")
dead = filter(r -> !r.survived, res); alive = filter(r -> r.survived, res)
scatter!(ax1, [r.x for r in dead], [r.T for r in dead], color = :crimson)
scatter!(ax1, [r.x for r in alive], [r.T for r in alive], color = :white,
         strokecolor = :teal, strokewidth = 1.5)
scatter!(ax2, [r.x for r in res], [r.lag for r in res],
         color = [r.survived ? :teal : :crimson for r in res])
fig
```

Populations that survive keep pace: their lag per generation is close to zero. Once the
environment moves faster than they can respond, the lag grows every generation and the
population dies, sooner the faster the change. For this
parameter set every population survived 2000 generations at rates up to about 6% of a
phenotypic standard deviation per generation, and every one died at about 7% and above.
Surviving 2000 generations is not surviving indefinitely, though: the paper ran its
populations for up to 240,000 generations, and its estimate of the sustainable rate,
about 3% of a standard deviation per generation, comes from the populations that lasted
that long. The [replication vignette](../09_replicating_pagel_2025/09_replicating_pagel_2025.qmd)
maps the boundary across the paper's whole parameter space.

## Fluctuating optima

Field environments change noisily, not along a straight line. Two more move types,
which QTSim lacks, let the optimum fluctuate around a linear trend of $d$ per
generation, starting from its value $\theta_0$ at generation $t_0$ =
`MoveFitnessSDGen`:

- `:periodic`: $\theta_t = \theta_0 + d(t - t_0) + A \sin(2\pi (t - t_0)/P)$, with
  amplitude $A$ = `MoveAmplitude` and period $P$ = `MovePeriod`;
- `:red_noise`: $\theta_t = \theta_0 + d(t - t_0) + \varepsilon_t$, where $\varepsilon$ is
  stationary AR(1) noise with standard deviation $\sigma$ = `MoveNoiseSD` and
  autocorrelation $\rho$ = `MoveAutocorr`:
  $\varepsilon_t = \rho\,\varepsilon_{t-1} + \sigma\sqrt{1-\rho^2}\,\xi_t$.

Once its genetic variance has settled, a large population's mean follows the optimum as
$\bar z_{t+1} = \bar z_t + \beta(\theta_t - \bar z_t)$, with
$\beta = V_G/(V_G + V_s)$ and $V_s = \omega^2 + V_E$. This linear filter tracks a slow
cycle with a delay of about $1/\beta$ generations, damps a fast one, and chases noise
that has already moved on. `periodic_response`, `red_noise_lag_var` and `expected_lag2`
give its steady response [@BurgerLynch1995]. A population under strong selection
($\omega = 0.3$, one locus) shows it in a few thousand generations. The three moves below
share the trend, and the cycle and the noise have the same variance,
$A^2/2 = \sigma^2$.

```{julia}
import Catlab                       # run_moments is part of the categorical layer
c = Params(PopSize = 1000, Ploidy = 2, NoQTL = 1, NoGenerations = 3000, PhenotypeVar = 0.02,
           Heritability = 0.5, MutationScalar = 0.02, MutationRatePerGamete = 0.5,
           InitFitnessSD = 0.3, MoveFitnessSDGen = 1000, MoveFitnessSD = 0.001)
fluct = [("linear, d = 0.001", Params(c; MoveType = :continuous)),
         ("periodic, A = 0.1, P = 200", Params(c; MoveType = :periodic, MoveAmplitude = 0.1, MovePeriod = 200.0)),
         ("red noise, σ = 0.071, ρ = 0.95", Params(c; MoveType = :red_noise, MoveNoiseSD = 0.1 / √2,
                                                  MoveAutocorr = 0.95))]
frun = [(name, q, simulate(q; seed = 7)) for (name, q) in fluct]
nothing
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-fluctuating
#| fig-cap: "The optimum (gray) and the mean phenotype (colour) under three moves that share a trend of 0.001 per generation from generation 1000. Dashed: the prediction of the moments lowering (`run_moments`; by default the rare-alleles closure, whose variance here is within 2% of the Gaussian model's), given the run's own optimum for red noise."
fig = Figure(size = (960, 300))
for (j, ((name, q, r), col)) in enumerate(zip(frun, (:crimson, :navy, :teal)))
    ax = Axis(fig[1, j], xlabel = "generation", ylabel = j == 1 ? "phenotype / optimum" : "",
              title = name, limits = ((900, 3000), nothing))
    m = q.MoveType === :red_noise ? run_moments(q; optimum = r.theta) : run_moments(q)
    lines!(ax, r.gen, r.theta, color = :gray)
    lines!(ax, r.gen, r.pheno_mean, color = col)
    lines!(ax, m.gen, m.pheno_mean, color = :black, linestyle = :dash)
end
fig
```

Averaged over eight runs each and over generations 1500 to 2999, the mean squared lag
is close to the prediction at the runs' genetic variance. Drift adds about the same small
amount to each, because it moves the mean at random, so it shows most in the small lag
behind the steady trend. The load, the loss of log mean fitness to the lag, is
`lag_load`.

```{julia}
win(r) = findall(g -> 1500 <= g <= 2999, r.gen)
for (name, q) in fluct
    rs = [simulate(q; seed = s) for s in 1:8]
    lag2 = mean(mean((r.theta[win(r)] .- r.pheno_mean[win(r)]) .^ 2) for r in rs)
    VG = mean(mean(r.geno_var[win(r)]) for r in rs)
    surv = mean(mean(r.nsurv[win(r)]) for r in rs)
    @printf("%-32s mean squared lag %.5f (theory %.5f)   load %.4f   survivors %.0f\n",
            name, lag2, expected_lag2(q; VG), lag_load(q; VG), surv)
end
```

At the same variance of the optimum, the cycle of period 200 costs more than the steady
trend but less than noise with a correlation time of about 20 generations, which
changes faster than the population can follow. The gain of the response, the ratio of
the mean's amplitude to the optimum's, falls as the period shortens:

```{julia}
#| label: fig-gain
#| fig-cap: "The gain of the mean phenotype's response to a periodic optimum (A = 0.1, no trend) against the period, in three runs per period (points), and the linear filter's prediction at the runs' genetic variance (line)."
periods = [25.0, 50.0, 100.0, 200.0, 400.0, 800.0, 1600.0]
gjobs = [(P, s) for P in periods for s in 1:3]
gres = Vector{Any}(undef, length(gjobs))
Threads.@threads :greedy for k in eachindex(gjobs)
    P, s = gjobs[k]
    q = Params(c; MoveType = :periodic, MoveFitnessSD = 0.0, MoveAmplitude = 0.1, MovePeriod = P,
               NoGenerations = 4200)
    r = simulate(q; seed = 50 + k)
    w = findall(>=(1000 + 1200), r.gen); t = r.gen[w] .- 1000
    X = hcat(sin.(2π .* t ./ P), cos.(2π .* t ./ P), ones(length(t)))
    a, b, _ = X \ r.pheno_mean[w]
    gres[k] = (; P, gain = hypot(a, b) / 0.1, VG = mean(r.geno_var[w]))
end
VGg = mean(r.VG for r in gres)
fig = Figure(size = (520, 340))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1], xscale = log10, xlabel = "period P (generations)", ylabel = "gain")
Ps = exp.(range(log(20), log(2000), 100))
lines!(ax, Ps, [periodic_response(P; VG = VGg, Vs = selection_variance(c)).gain for P in Ps], color = :gray)
scatter!(ax, [r.P for r in gres], [r.gain for r in gres], color = :navy)
fig
```
